Trackers are installed not by the tracker companies but by EPC installers, who receive training and field services from the tracker companies. Tracker companies may manufacture some components, but much of the manufacturing is done by third-party suppliers. Tracker companies balance the cost of tracker component production against the speed with which they can get components to an installation site, which can result in manufacturing locations that are more expensive but closer to demand, such as the United States and Mexico (Basore and Feldman 2022a). This section provides an overview of single-axis tracker systems and some of their key components (Figure 46). Subsequent parts this section provide additional detail on the supply chain for other components: torque tubes, fasteners/clamps, piles and rebar, and racking/rails. Figure 46. Simplified supply chain diagram for single-axis trackers 4.2.1 Technology Trends for Trackers Trackers are available in a variety of configurations (Table 10). The greatest distinction is between single-axis and dual-axis designs. Single-axis trackers have one rotational axis, which simplifies the mechanical design and reduces costs but limits the tracker’s ability to optimize incident sunlight. Dual-axis trackers, in contrast, employ a more complex and expensive rotational system to keep the PV modules perpendicular to the sun and thus maximize incident 68 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. sunlight. As shown in Table 10, single-axis designs constitute almost the entire U.S. and global tracker markets. This report addresses only single-axis products. Among single-axis designs, several options are available: single-row, dual-row, and centralized (Table 10). These options present trade-offs between the flexibility offered by systems with independent rows and the installation efficiencies and reliability (because fewer actuators are required per row) offered by systems with linked rows. The comparative popularity of these options also has implications for the tracker supply chain, because each requires different types and amounts of materials and components. In 2023, single-row trackers—which are most flexible in terms of smart tracking and installation at sites with difficult geometries or terrain— had captured about two-thirds of U.S. and global market shares. Because each tracker company tends to focus on one or two tracker designs, changes in market share by company are related to changes in market share by technology. For example, among leading U.S.-headquartered tracker companies, Nextracker focuses on single-row designs, GameChange Solar on single-row designs (primarily) and dual-row designs (secondarily), and Array Technologies on centralized designs (primarily) and dual-row designs (secondarily) (Joe Shangraw 2024d, 2024c; Joe Shangraw and Shen 2025). Several additional tracker technology trends have supply chain implications as well: • Smart tracking requires increasingly sophisticated controller hardware and software to combine artificial intelligence algorithms, real-time site data, and weather forecasts for applications such as minimizing row-to-row shading, positioning modules optimally during cloudy conditions, and stowing modules during wind and hail events (Joe Shangraw 2024d). • One-in-portrait (1P) module mounting has constituted about 80% of the global market recently, with 2P constituting most of the rest 20%.
